title: Q4 Product Roadmap Review

summary.overview: Jordan led a cross-functional review of the Q4 roadmap with Hannah, Priya, Sofia, and David. The group ranked candidate projects by customer demand, effort, and revenue impact, and agreed on search, a ticketing integration, and enterprise single sign-on as the top three. Mobile apps and a public API were deferred to Q1. David shared that three deals are blocked on single sign-on, and Hannah asked the team to keep a quarter-end review so scope can be cut if estimates grow. The meeting ended with owners assigned to write one-page briefs for each committed project.

action_items.text: Write a one-page brief for meeting search including scope, metrics, and risks
Estimate single sign-on work and identify the identity providers to support first
List the three blocked deals with revenue amounts and required SSO providers
Produce design explorations for the ticketing integration settings page
Schedule the end-of-quarter scope review with leadership

transcript.summary: Agreed on how projects would be ranked: demand, effort, and revenue impact.

transcript: Thanks everyone for joining. The goal today is to leave with a committed Q4 roadmap, meaning three or four projects we're confident about, and a clear list of what we are deliberately not doing. I'd like us to be disciplined about that second part.
Support that. Last quarter we committed to six things and finished four. I'd rather commit to fewer and deliver them well.

Agreed. To keep this objective, I suggest we rank each candidate on three dimensions. Customer demand, which is how often it comes up in sales and support. Effort, in engineering weeks. And revenue impact, meaning new deals or retention.
Can I add a fourth? Risk. Some projects have a lot of unknowns, and an estimate of six weeks might actually be twelve. I'd like us to tag anything with high uncertainty.
Good addition. Let's mark each project as low, medium, or high risk. I've got eight candidates on the list, so let's go through them one at a time and I'll capture the scores as we go.
Before we start, can I ask whether design effort is counted somewhere? Some of these need a lot of design work and it shows up before engineering starts.
Yes, I'll include design weeks in the effort number, so it's the total cost across the team.

transcript.summary: Highest-demand request; strong consensus to commit.

transcript: First candidate is search across all meetings. From customer interviews, it came up in almost every one. People can't find a decision made two months ago.
I'd call it the number one question in demos too. Prospects ask, can I search what was said across all meetings, and when I say not yet, I can feel the interest drop.

The technical foundation is already there. We've built a full-text index on the transcript, so the backend is mostly the query API, ranking, and snippets. I'd estimate four to five weeks including frontend.
Design is about two weeks. The results page, filters by date and speaker, and the empty states. I already have rough layouts of the results list.
What does success look like? I'd like a measurable goal and not just that it shipped.

I'd propose that thirty percent of weekly active users run at least one search within a month of launch, and that retention for those users is measurably higher than for those who don't. I'll write that into the brief.
Risk is low to medium. Ranking quality is the unknown, but we can launch with a simple version and tune.
That's an easy yes from me. Search is committed.

transcript.summary: Deals blocked on SSO make it the second commitment; scope to be estimated.

transcript: Second candidate is enterprise single sign-on. David, you've been raising this one.

Yes. Right now three active deals are blocked on it. Their security teams will not approve a tool that requires separate passwords. Combined, those deals are about three hundred ten thousand dollars in annual contract value.
That's more than I realized. Over a third of our Q4 bookings target is waiting on this.

Engineering effort is the question. Basic SAML support is not complicated, but the details around provisioning users, handling different identity providers, and testing each one tend to eat time. I'd say six to eight weeks for two engineers, medium risk.
Could we shrink the scope? For instance, support only the two most common identity providers at first?
Yes, that's what I'd recommend. If we pick the providers that those three deals use, we can cover most of the demand. I'll work out a firm estimate once David shares which providers they need.
I'll pull the list today. I believe two of the three use the same provider, but I want to confirm before I promise anything.
Make it committed, with scope to be confirmed. I want to be able to tell those customers a date within the week.

transcript.summary: Ticketing integration committed; mobile app and public API deferred.

transcript: Third is the ticketing integration, where action items from a meeting become tickets in the customer's system. This one is a big theme for logistics and operations customers.
It's the most requested integration by far. Three of the last ten prospects mentioned it unprompted.

If we do one well, it also becomes a template for the others. Effort is about five weeks for the first, with a lot of that being the authentication and field mapping, which we reuse for the later ones.

There's a design question too. Mapping fields between our action items and the ticket fields can get complicated quickly. I want to explore a simple settings page, something like choose a project and a default type, and keep advanced mapping out of the first version.
That's the right instinct. Hannah, any concern about doing three large projects at once?
Capacity is my concern. Search is five weeks, SSO is up to eight, and the integration is five. We have a limited team, and I want to make sure we're not at a hundred percent allocation.
Right now we'd be about ninety percent allocated with some overlap, which leaves a little room for support and bugs. It's tight, though. I'd not add a fourth.
Then let's talk about what falls out. The two next on my list were the mobile apps and the public API.
I'd push back a little on the API. A couple of enterprise prospects asked for it. But when I dug in, they would be fine with the ticketing integration as an interim, so I think it can wait.
And mobile? We hear about it occasionally, but I think people mostly want to read summaries on their phones, and the responsive web does that decently.
Agreed. A native app is a big investment, and I'd want to first improve the mobile web experience, which is much cheaper.
I'm happy to defer both to Q1, as long as we write down why, so we don't relitigate it in two months.

I'll document it in the roadmap notes, with the reasons and the signals that would change our mind. For example, if mobile web usage passes a certain share or three or more customers cite it as a reason for churn.

transcript.chapter: Risks, scope control, and next steps
transcript.summary: Quarter-end scope review and owners for each project brief.

transcript: One more thing I'd like to put in place. A mid-quarter review where we look at actual progress against estimates and decide what to cut. Last quarter we noticed the slip too late.
I like that. Let's say six weeks in, we check each project, and if any is more than twenty percent over its estimate, we decide explicitly whether to cut scope, add people, or move the date.
That works for engineering. The key is that cutting scope is a normal outcome and not seen as a failure.
Agreed, I'll put that on the calendar and invite the full leadership group, so they're aware of the trade-offs before the quarter ends.
Can I also ask that we agree on the sequence? If search ships first, I can use the learnings to inform the integration design, and SSO has little UI so it doesn't compete for my time.
Yes, the plan I'd suggest is search starts now, SSO starts in parallel with Priya's team, and the ticketing integration starts in week three once design has explored the settings page.
That sequencing makes sense and keeps people from being pulled in too many directions.
From sales, I'd want a shareable roadmap I can use with prospects, but without dates I can't keep. Can we agree on quarter-level commitments and keep the language careful?
Yes, quarter-level only. Jordan, can the brief include a short external-facing summary that David can use?

I'll add one. Let me recap the owners. I'm writing the search brief and the roadmap notes. Priya estimates SSO. David lists the blocked deals. Sofia explores the integration settings design. Hannah schedules the mid-quarter review.
That matches my notes. I'll have the SSO estimate once David sends the list.
I'll send the list within the hour, since I already have most of it.
Thank you all. This was a productive session. I feel much better about the quarter.
Thanks, everyone. I'll circulate the notes and the briefs this week.
